title: Training Variational Quantum Algorithms Is NP-Hard, Even Locally
authors: Dax Enshan Koh, Triscia Mundo, Iosif Sakos, Antonios Varvitsiotis
abstract: Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) generally rely on classical optimization to train parameterized quantum circuits. This training seeks to minimize an objective function, and its efficiency is central to the practical success of these algorithms. However, globally minimizing such training objectives over the circuit parameters is known to be $\mathsf{NP}$-hard, limiting the prospect of general guarantees for efficient training. In this Letter, we prove that even the weaker task of finding a local minimum of such VQA training objectives is strongly $\mathsf{NP}$-hard, including when the objective admits efficient classical evaluation. Moreover, we show that this hardness persists even for the task of finding a parameter vector within $\ell_p$-distance strictly less than $π/2$ of some local minimizer, for every $p\geq 1$. Our central technical result is that approximating a local minimizer of a Hermitian trigonometric polynomial is strongly $\mathsf{NP}$-hard. By explicitly constructing quantum circuits whose training objectives reproduce these hard instances, we obtain a polynomial-time reduction to VQA training. Our results establish a fundamental computational barrier to variational quantum training: even reaching the vicinity of a local minimum remains hard in the worst case.
summary: This paper proves that training Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) is computationally hard, showing that even finding a local minimum of the objective function is strongly NP-hard. The authors achieve this by reducing the problem from the known hard Stable Set problem to the minimization of a trigonometric polynomial, which is then mapped directly onto a VQA training objective. This establishes a fundamental worst-case computational barrier for variational quantum optimization.
main_problem: The paper investigates the computational hardness of training Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs), specifically focusing on the difficulty of finding local minima of the training objective function.
main_result: It proves that finding a local minimum of a VQA training objective, or even approximating a point near it, is strongly NP-hard in the worst case.
method: The proof uses a polynomial-time reduction from the Stable Set problem, transforming the hard combinatorial optimization problem into the minimization of a Hermitian trigonometric polynomial, which is then mapped to the VQA objective function.
model_or_system: The model is the VQA, which trains parameterized quantum circuits by minimizing an objective function $F(	heta) = \langle 0|U(	heta)^\dagger H U(	heta)|0angle$. The hardness is shown even for simple circuits using single-qubit rotations and commuting observables.
key_observables: The training objective function $F(	heta)$, the location of local minimizers $	heta^*$, and the $\ell_p$-distance to these minimizers.
important_parameters: The circuit parameters $	heta \in \mathbb{R}^n$, the distance metric $\ell_p$ ($p \ge 1$), and the size of the graph $G$ used in the reduction.
main_assumptions: The hardness result is established for the worst-case scenario, and the proof relies on a dichotomy related to the stable set size $\alpha(G)$ versus a parameter $k$.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the separation of possible local minimizers in the parameter space for the hard trigonometric polynomial instance, and Figure 2 shows the mapping between local minimizers under the trigonometric substitution $T(	heta)$.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the computational barrier by first reducing the Stable Set problem to minimizing a Hermitian trigonometric polynomial, and then constructing an explicit quantum circuit whose VQA training objective reproduces this hard instance.
why_interesting: This work provides a fundamental theoretical barrier, suggesting that even local optimization in VQAs is computationally intractable in the worst case, which is crucial for understanding the limits of near-term quantum computation.
